items.title: PTI's 'doors are open' to Fazl's offer to play a role in breaking deadlock with govt: Junaid Akbar
items.description: PTI MNA Junaid Akbar on Thursday said that Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman had offered to play a role in ending the deadlock between the government and opposition and the PTI’s “doors are open” to it. Over the weekend, the government and opposition held two rounds of talks ahead of the PTI’s march, initially planned for Islamabad, to demand the release of jailed party founder Imran Khan. The talks, however, ended in a stalemate, with counterterrorism policies and access to Imran emerging as two major sticking points. Speaking on the Geo News programme ‘ Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath ’ on Thursday evening, Akbar said Fazl had contacted the PTI leadership and expressed the desire to play his part in ending the deadlock, if agreed to by the party. “We are political people and we understand that the issue can be solved with dialogue,” he added, emphasising that “the intention of this should be dialogue” rather than an attempt to trap the PTI. “Whatever role he wants to play in any purposeful dialogue that happens, our doors are open,” he said, adding that the party had been open to this “from the start”. “We have never run from dialogue; we want the solution to be found through negotiations,” Akbar said, but added that the party was not given “space” for this. In response to a question, he said that no framework had been put forward by Fazl regarding his role in the negotiations, although he noted that the JUI-F chief had been in touch with PTI leadership while he was away for Umrah. While the MNA repeatedly stressed that the PTI’s “doors were open” to negotiations, he asserted that this could not be done by force. “Our doors have always been open, but we will not sit down for negotiations at gunpoint, nor will we agree to them; no one can force us into negotiations,” he said. The MNA added, “We are ready to sit down with anyone who wants to; we ask that you either convince us, or at least listen to what we have to say.” Separately, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif also appeared to be confirming that efforts to restart negotiations between the Centre and the opposition were under way. “I wish a positive result comes out of the efforts of those involved in the talks. But, I have little hope. Those making efforts are my brothers and friends, and I wish them well. We should always avoid unnecessary confrontation,” he said during ARY News programme ‘ Khabar Muhammad Malick Ke Saath ’. Discussing the matter, he also remarked that Fazl was seemingly involved, either directly or indirectly. On Wednesday, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah also said “the doors for talks are open”, recalling Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s remarks from Tuesday calling on the PTI leadership to sit down with the government for dialogue and abandon their protest plans. However, he also warned that the PTI could pressure the government into accepting its demands by holding the state “hostage” and creating political instability. Prior to that, a delegation of opposition parties called on Fazl, who advised the government after the meeting not to obstruct the PTI long march heading towards Islamabad, as protests were a democratic right enjoyed by all political parties. Speaking to the media alongside opposition leaders outside his residence, the JUI-F leader also urged the government to trust the PTI’s intention regarding a peaceful protest. When political parties say they will remain peaceful, their word should be trusted, he said in a comment on measures taken by the government to stop the PTI protesters from entering the federal capital. A delegation of the government also visited Fazl on Wednesday amid reports about the possibility of his involvement as a mediator between the two sides. The hours-long negotiations between the government and the opposition ended in a deadlock on Sunday during a second round of talks. The meeting at Parliament House began on Saturday afternoon and continued into the wee hours of Sunday, with discussions focusing on the PTI’s protest march. After the talks collapsed, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi accused Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi of “sabotaging” the negotiations, saying that he had changed the draft of the agreement despite what had been agreed to earlier. However, PTI leaders, presenting the opposition’s stance on the failed talks, declared that reconciliation with the government was not possible without including incarcerated party founder Imran Khan in the dialogue process. They said that another reason for the failure of the talks was that the government was not willing to pursue a collective strategy against terrorism. And following the breakdown of the talks, the PTI launched its long march.

items.title: National Security Implications of the Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2026 (Act 1168) of Ghana
items.description: Ghana’s current security situation is characterised by interconnected threats such as terrorism, violent extremism, organised crime, cybercrime, espionage, pandemics and climate insecurity. Such a situation requires the establishment of security institutions capable of providing an integrated security and intelligence system with effective legal structures that allow for an efficient reaction to security threats. For this reason, national security has moved from traditional security and defence to security and intelligence governance and national resilience. Ghana enacted the Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2026 (Act 1168) to replace the Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2000 (Act 1030). The former modernises Ghana’s security and intelligence architecture by strengthening regional and local security governance, establishing clearly defined intelligence agencies, reinforcing the role of the National Security Coordinator and streamlining the executive oversight of national security. The Act also promotes intelligence coordination, professionalism, democratic oversight and accountability within the national security sector. This paper analyses the effects of the national security components of Act 1168 from the Realist school of thought, Human Security Theory, SSG and the WoG approaches. The paper demonstrates that Act 1168 not only provides for institutional reforms but also offers an overall framework to enhance the strategic coordination of security, intelligence management, counterterrorism, democratic governance, cybersecurity, crisis management, national resilience and regional cooperation. The paper concludes with implementation difficulties and recommendations for policy improvements of Ghana’s national security structure. Theoretical Framework The paper applies Realism, Human Security Theory, SSG and the WoG Approach to examine the national security components of Ghana’s Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2026 (Act 1168). These theories collectively highlight the role of the state in protecting national interests, monitoring the evolution of security threats, accountability of security structures and the requirements for coordinated government response to security challenges. Realism forms the traditional basis of national security that perceives the state as the most important actor to secure its sovereignty, territorial integrity and constitutional structure amid an unpredictable international setting. From this perspective, Act 1168 enhances Ghana’s capacity to respond to security threats by providing a legal framework to handle intelligence activities and security decision-making. This includes the National Security Council, security and intelligence organisations and the Office of the National Security Coordinator, which collectively enhance the capabilities of the state to secure national interests through intelligence and policy execution. However, Realism fails to offer an exhaustive account of security threats in the modern world because certain security threats are beyond the realm of military affairs. The Human Security Theory advances the concept of security by focusing on individuals and communities as the focus of security policies. The theory recognises that insecurity potentially arises from terrorism, organised crime, communal conflicts, pandemics, environmental degradation, cybercrime and other non-traditional threats. Act 1168, as provided in Act 526 (1996) and Act 1030 (2000), reflects this broader conception by establishing REGSECs and DISECs to provide early warning, local threat assessment and coordinated responses to local security challenges. The Act, therefore, promotes preventive security by coordinating national security institutions with decentralised governance structures, thereby improving the capacity of states to address threats before escalation. The SSG framework serves as the main institutional framework for assessing the relevance of Act 1168. The framework focuses on the principles of legality, civilian control, accountability, efficacy, and mandate clarity. The Act establishes the intelligence agencies, the Office of the National Security Coordinator, and decentralised security councils; hence, it ensures clear responsibilities of the institutions and good governance and coordination in security management. The effectiveness of national security does not depend solely on capacity, but also on the institutions operating under the rule of law and proper oversight mechanisms. The SSG framework incorporates the WoG approach through which security challenges demand integrated solutions from stakeholder institutions. Modern threats are often multifaceted in that they cross over defence, intelligence, policing, immigration, local government and emergency management, among others. This is evident in the design of Act 1168, which creates systems for cooperation, intelligence gathering and planning among national, regional and district security institutions. These theories form an overarching framework which can be applied to assess the national security issues associated with Act 1168. Realism helps explain why it is necessary to defend the state, while Human Security expands the concept of security to incorporate the security of citizens. The SSG Theory emphasises good governance, effectiveness and accountability. Finally, the WoG approach emphasises the necessity of strategic coordination. This approach can be applied to the study of the role of Act 1168 in improving strategic coordination, intelligence cooperation, counterterrorism and national resilience. Strengthening Strategic Coordination Coordination is pivotal in the national security structure due to the multifaceted nature of contemporary threats. Such issues as terrorism, extremism, cybercrime, organised crime, maritime insecurity, illegal mining, health emergencies and environmental disasters require coordination efforts that cannot be achieved by individual organisations. It is for this reason that the Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2026 (Act 1168) is relevant to national security because it provides a legal structure for intelligence coordination, policy formulation, planning and crisis management among security agencies. Firstly, the Act enhances coordination through the National Security Council, which acts as the apex institution mandated to harmonise national security policies and strategic directions. The National Security Council is chaired by the President of the Republic of Ghana and comprises political, defence and high-level intelligence and security officials. The National Security Council ensures executive decision-making is based on intelligence analysis and planning. Secondly, the Act enhances coordination through the Office of the National Security Coordinator. The National Security Coordinator coordinates activities among the various intelligence and security agencies, advises the National Security Council and facilitates the integration of intelligence. This coordination is critical because a lack of coordination may arise from institutional rivalry, overlapping functions and fragmentation in intelligence reporting. Such coordination increases the efficiency of threat analysis and enables the government to make decisions and allocate resources based on available intelligence. Moreover, Act 1168 defines the responsibilities of principal intelligence institutions of Ghana. Internal, external and signal intelligence agencies perform different but complementary roles, making their operations more efficient because the necessity of collaboration eliminates duplication. Coordination among these three agencies becomes critical in situations where threats have internal, external and technological components. Security decentralisation to the regional and district levels through the establishment of REGSECs and DISECs ensures coordination with the national government on local-level security challenges. This enables information from the local level to be relayed to the national level, while enforcing national security policies. Regional Ministers and District Chief Executives chair the REGSECs and DISECs, respectively. REGSECs and DISECs ensure horizontal coordination among the police, military, immigration, fire service, intelligence agencies, local authorities and other related agencies. The combined assessment of security situations assists in coordinated response to communal strife, chieftaincy disputes, border insecurity, terrorism, disasters and public health crises. By combining the skills of the various agencies, local-level security councils become more effective in managing emergency situations. In line with the theoretical perspectives, Act 1168 represents an example of both WoG and SSG perspectives. The key message in both of these theoretical perspectives is that the solution to any security challenge must involve collaboration among stakeholder institutions, not isolated solutions at the level of individual agencies. The Act also encourages a human security framework since it gives security agencies the mandate to respond to threats to the safety and wellbeing of citizens that extend beyond military considerations. However, for these coordination frameworks to succeed, they must depend on proper implementation. Bureaucratic rivalry, politicisation, inadequate information-sharing processes, overlapping responsibilities and inadequate analysis potentially compromise their effectiveness. Therefore, the need exists for Ghana to develop communication networks that are compatible across security agencies, joint training programmes and exercises, among others. Intelligence Collection and Analysis Tied in closely with the reinforcement of strategic coordination is the improvement in intelligence gathering and analysis, which is a major national security implication of the Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2026 (Act 1168). Although strategic coordination offers the organisational structure that facilitates collaboration among security players, intelligence gathering and analysis offer the data required for decision-making and threat anticipation. Therefore, the efficiency of Ghana’s national security structure depends on the capacity of the structure to provide timely and accurate information for policy formulation and operational purposes. Act 1168 strengthens Ghana’s national intelligence system by establishing a clear legal and institutional framework for the collection, analysis, coordination and dissemination of intelligence. Together with Act 1040, Act 1168 recognises three principal intelligence agencies, the Internal Intelligence Agency, External Intelligence Agency and the Signals Intelligence Agency, with clear mandates that collectively address domestic, foreign and technological dimensions of national security. This legal classification encourages specialisation and eliminates duplication of efforts and competition that typically exist within a fragmented intelligence community. Additionally, the Act bolsters intelligence effectiveness through the coordination function of the National Security Coordinator and the National Security Council. With the provision of such coordinated mechanisms as the National Security Coordinator and the National Security Council, the coordination of information exchange between intelligence agencies and other security agencies becomes possible, thus producing integrated intelligence assessments for decision-making. Instead of using separate intelligence reports, the government can make use of comprehensive intelligence that includes information from different sources, which improves decision-making and effectiveness in assessing threats. Enhanced intelligence analysis improves Ghana’s ability to deal with complex and interrelated security issues. Contemporary issues, including violent extremism, terrorism, cybercrime, transnational organised crime, maritime security, illegal mining, human trafficking and foreign influence, often exceed the jurisdictional mandate of individual organisations. Act 1168 encourages intelligence fusion through cooperation among intelligence agencies, law enforcement bodies and the Ghana Armed Forces through a Joint Intelligence Committee chaired by the National Security Coordinator. This collaboration enables intelligence analysts to detect emerging trends and take appropriate preventive action before escalation. The decentralised security framework provided for under Act 1168 enhances intelligence gathering through the incorporation of REGSECs and DISECs into the national security framework. These councils provide a useful source of intelligence gathered from the districts and regions since they gather information on communal disputes, chieftaincy disputes, cross-border crimes, terrorism threats, environmental security threats, among others. The transmission of such information to national security structures enhances Ghana’s early warning framework. From the Realist perspective, the role of intelligence is to enhance the ability of the state to defend its sovereignty and interests by minimising strategic uncertainty. This idea is supplemented by the concept of Human Security Theory, in which intelligence should not only detect threats to the country but also threats to the security and wellbeing of citizens. SSG, on the other hand, highlights that intelligence operations must be undertaken according to the rule of law. Enhancement of Counterterrorism Capacity: It is evident that the enhancements made to intelligence gathering and analysis through the Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2026 (Act 1168) have implications in terms of the counterterrorism capabilities of Ghana. It is important to note that effective counterterrorism requires intelligence, coordination and decision-making. The introduction of Act 1168 provides a better institutional setup to ensure prevention, detection and response to the threat of terrorism. This is especially important in view of the growing number of violent extremist groups in the Sahel region and the likelihood of terrorist spillover into West African nations. The Act improves Ghana’s capacity to prevent terrorist attacks through institutionalised cooperation among the Internal Intelligence Agency, External Intelligence Agency, Signals Intelligence Agency, Ghana Armed Forces, Ghana Police Service and other security agencies. Terrorist groups exploit porous borders, cyber tools, international criminal activities and local conflicts to recruit and finance their operations. Thus, no single institution possesses sufficient capability to address these multidimensional threats independently. The Act, therefore, strengthens national security by providing statutory mechanisms for intelligence sharing, joint threat assessments and coordinated operational planning across agencies. The Act also strengthens the country’s early warning and preventive capabilities. Intelligence generated through national agencies, together with information obtained from REGSECs and DISECs, enables the government to identify indicators of radicalisation, terrorist financing, cross-border infiltration and violent extremist activities before attacks occur. The proposed preventative strategy aligns with the UN philosophy to combat terrorism through early action, enhanced intelligence cooperation and institutional integration as opposed to military action alone. One other implication of the Act 1168 is intelligence fusion and strategic analysis. Terrorist threats usually arise from the combination of crime, money laundering, arms dealing and ideology. Intelligence analysis involves merging information from different agencies for overall threat assessment. Similarly, the UN Office of Counter-Terrorism identifies inter-agency “Fusion Centre” approaches as international best practice for strengthening the capacity of African states to prevent and counter terrorism through coordinated intelligence analysis. Ghana participates in this capacity-building initiative. Therefore, the country has established the National Counter-Terrorism Fusion Centre as part of this approach. Additionally, Act 1168 supports Ghana’s regional counterterrorism cooperation. The threat of terrorism in West Africa remains transnational and, therefore, calls for intelligence sharing among neighbouring countries. The Act enhances Ghana’s ability to collaborate with regional bodies such as ECOWAS and the AU through national institutions to coordinate intelligence and implement related policies. Ghana stresses the need for increased cooperation among regions on intelligence and counterterrorism operations. Realism provides an understanding that the state has an obligation to create institutions that can protect the state’s sovereignty from the danger of terrorism. On the other hand, the Human Security Theory expands the obligation of the state by acknowledging that terrorism is a threat to the security of individuals and society. SSG stresses the importance of establishing statutory institutions that operate under democratic accountability, and the WoG stresses the importance of coordinated action among various institutions. Strengthening Democratic Governance Although the Act enhances the country’s ability to fight terrorism, the national security implication of the Act is improving democratic governance. Effective counterterrorism requires robust security institutions; however, sustainable national security depends equally on ensuring institutions operate within a constitutional framework characterised by legality, accountability and the respect for the rule of law. The Act, therefore, seeks to balance the operational effectiveness of intelligence agencies with democratic oversight, thereby reinforcing public confidence in Ghana’s security architecture, The Act strengthens democratic governance by providing a comprehensive statutory framework that unequivocally defines the mandates, functions and reporting relationships of Ghana’s intelligence agencies and coordinating institutions. By replacing the fragmented legal arrangements in previous Acts, Act 1168 establishes greater legal certainty regarding the roles of the National Security Council, the National Security Coordinator, the Internal Intelligence Agency, the External Intelligence Agency, the Signals Intelligence Agency and the REGSECs and DISECs. Unambiguous institutional responsibilities reduce overlapping mandates, minimise arbitrary exercise of power and improve accountability within the national security sector. An equally important implication is the strengthening of civilian control over the security and intelligence sector. The Act places intelligence agencies under the strategic supervision of the National Security Council and provides executive democratic control and oversight through a minister responsible for National Security. These provisions guarantee security agencies are subordinate to the democratically elected civilian government and act under the terms prescribed by the law. Such systems are likely to foster transparency and good governance. Act 1168 promotes good democratic governance through enhanced legislative oversight. The provision for reporting on the national security strategy ensures the legislature can oversee the executive oversight of the operations of the security sector while still being able to protect the confidentiality of certain operations. Democratic control and oversight are important elements of intelligence governance because they ensure accountability and professionalism. Also, the requirement for the Constitution and the other relevant laws to govern intelligence activities under Act 1168 ensures the rule of law is reinforced. This helps to ensure intelligence activities respect human rights while providing for an effective response to threats. In democratic societies, confidence in intelligence institutions not only depends on the institutions’ ability to provide security but also on their ability to observe legality and civil liberties. The SSG Theory is the main paradigm through which these changes can be perceived. This theory underscores the necessity of security-sector institutions operating under democratic supervision, civilian oversight, transparency and accountability. The WoG Theory is compatible with the SSG because it recognises that good democratic governance requires coordination among executive-branch institutions, the legislature, local governments, and the security agencies. The Human Security Theory also demonstrates the fact that the people’s confidence in state institutions constitutes an element of security. [i] Protection of Human Rights In addition to strengthening democratic governance, Act 1168 has further consequences for human rights, which is a vital component of national security. It is not possible for democratic governance to survive if security and intelligence agencies operate outside of the law. On the other hand, national security requires trust based on democratic security governance. [ii] Consequently, the Act is geared at striking a balance between operational efficiency of the security and intelligence organisations on one hand and the rights and freedoms provided for in the 1992 Constitution of Ghana on the other. The Act further enhances the protection of human rights through the creation of a statutory regime that defines the role, mandate and powers of the intelligence and security bodies in Ghana. Through clear mandates and powers, abuse of authority can be minimised since the intelligence services only operate within the scope of law. Legal certainty assumes even greater significance, as intelligence services have special powers regarding surveillance, intelligence operations and covert action, all of which require protection from abuse. Similarly, Act 1168 provides for enhanced accountability and oversight systems that protect individuals’ rights, as well as promote institutional legitimacy. By putting intelligence agencies under civilian control through the National Security Council, ministerial accountability and parliamentary reporting, the Act promotes democratic oversight of security agencies. Such oversight minimises instances of illegal arrest, politicisation of intelligence, intrusive surveillance and breaches of privacy, thereby ensuring public trust in national security agencies. As an international best practice, the significance of accountability and oversight systems cannot be overlooked either. The Act further safeguards human rights by encouraging intelligence-driven preventive security instead of an approach that overly relies on coercive solutions. Intelligence gathering and early warning mechanisms, coupled with the application of security networks, enable security organisations to prevent acts of terrorism, communal violence and organised crime from erupting into armed conflicts. The use of prevention reduces the need for emergency measures that potentially infringe on individual liberties and, thus, aligns with democratic principles and human security. The UN emphasises that human rights and the rule of law are an integral part of a counterterrorism strategy. Theoretically, Human Security Theory forms the main approach behind these reforms, which considers the protection of rights, dignity and well-being of individuals as major goals of national security. Additionally, SSG supports the Human Security Theory with emphasis on the relevance of legality, accountability and the observance of constitutional norms for creating efficient security organisations. Both theories indicate that the betterment of national security depends on the efficiency of security and intelligence services operating under the rule of law. Enhanced Cybersecurity The protection of human rights in relation to Ghana’s security architecture extends to cyberspace, where safeguarding personal information, privacy and critical information infrastructure is becoming a crucial component of national security. To ensure democratic governance and protect human rights, the Act further enhances the ability of Ghana to respond to cyberthreats through effective intelligence, interagency coordination and security governance. The Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), on the other hand, provides the main legislation in relation to cyberspace. Cyberthreats, including cyber espionage, ransomware, cyberterrorism, identity theft, misinformation campaigns and threats to critical information infrastructure, remain major national security issues. Act 1168 improves Ghana’s readiness through coordination between the intelligence agencies and related agencies. Through the National Security Council and the Office of the National Security Coordinator, Act 1168 ensures intelligence sharing and joint threat assessment and response. The Act also enhances the security of national critical infrastructure, including government information systems, financial institutions, telecommunications, energy and defence networks. Coordinated intelligence gathering directs agencies’ focus to emerging cyber threats that could become matters of national concern. Such coordinated efforts strengthen the National Cybersecurity Policy and Strategy of Ghana, which is based on the principles of intelligence sharing and multi-stakeholder collaboration for protecting national critical information infrastructure. Realism identifies the need to use cyberspace as a strategy in safeguarding the sovereignty and national interests of states. In relation to the Human Security Theory, there is also the need to safeguard the digital rights of individuals. The SSG paradigm stresses the fact that cyber intelligence operations must be conducted under the rule of law. The WoG concept stresses the need for cooperation among intelligence agencies, the Cyber Security Authority, law enforcement institutions and private-sector critical infrastructure operators. Protection of Critical National Infrastructure The enhancement of cybersecurity under Act 1168 naturally extends to the protection of Ghana’s critical national infrastructure, which is essential for national security, economic stability and public welfare. Critical infrastructure, including energy installations, telecommunications networks, transportation systems, financial institutions, ports, airports and water supply facilities, is increasingly vulnerable to terrorism, cyberattacks, espionage, sabotage and organised crime. [v] While the Ghana Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038) provides the regulatory framework for protecting critical information infrastructure, Act 1168 strengthens national security by integrating intelligence, strategic coordination and operational planning for the protection of these strategic assets. A major implication of Act 1168 is the promotion of intelligence-led infrastructure protection. Through the coordinated activities of the Internal Intelligence Agency and the Signals Intelligence Agency, security institutions are equipped to identify, assess and respond to threats before they materialise. Intelligence sharing through the National Security Council and the Office of the National Security Coordinator enhances risk assessment, and this, in turn, boosts national resilience to both physical and virtual threats. This Act also fosters interagency collaboration through cooperation among intelligence agencies, the Ghana Armed Forces, the Ghana Police Service, the Cyber Security Authority, sector regulators and operators of strategic infrastructure. Furthermore, regional and district security councils contribute to this process through intelligence gathering on the weaknesses of vital institutions and subsequent prevention measures. Realism highlights the significance of securing strategic infrastructure for state security and sovereignty. The Human Security Theory acknowledges that continuous access to basic utilities is an integral part of the well-being of the citizenry, while SSG and the WoG theories emphasise coordinated and intelligence-led protection of strategic national assets. [i] Stronger Crisis Management Safeguarding critical national infrastructure through Act 1168 enhances the ability to manage crises. Contemporary security crises, including terrorist attacks, cyber incidents, natural disasters, public health emergencies, communal conflicts and industrial accidents, often threaten critical infrastructure, hence requiring rapid, coordinated and multi-agency responses. [ii] Act 1168 provides an institutional framework that enables security institutions to anticipate, manage and recover from such crises through integrated intelligence, strategic coordination and decentralised decision-making. A major implication of the Act is the establishment of clear coordination mechanisms for crisis response. Regarding intelligence sharing, threat assessment and operational planning, the National Security Council, the Office of the National Security Coordinator and the regional and district security councils enable effective implementation of Act 1168 for the purpose of improving the coordination of decision-making and operations and reducing duplication. Furthermore, the decentralisation of security governance enhances crisis management. The regional and district security councils ensure early warning for the identification of potential threats in their respective jurisdictions, thereby coordinating response with the aid of the National Disaster Management Organisation prior to escalation. Based on the theoretical standpoint, the WoG concept is considered the primary paradigm through which these reforms may be explained, emphasising the idea that a complex crisis demands an integrated response from related agencies and civil and other government institutions. The SSG approach also stresses the significance of the presence of mandate, accountability and interagency coordination as elements of efficient crisis management. Support for National Security Strategy Implementation Act 1168 provides for improved crisis management systems as a robust basis for the review and implementation of Ghana’s National Security Strategy. The success of a national security strategy depends on the robust institutions tasked to implement the strategy. [i] The Act, therefore, provides for the review of the National Security Strategy within one year of the inauguration of a new Parliament. The Act also serves as a critical implementation instrument by providing the legal, institutional and administrative framework required to operationalise the objectives of the National Security Strategy. [ii] The Act aligns Ghana’s security institutions with a common strategic direction. National security policy coordination, intelligence assessments and response are achieved through the National Security Council and the Office of the National Security Coordinator. This ensures security institutions coordinate on meeting national objectives and not just organisational objectives. The Act improves implementation through decentralised security governance. Through the regional and district security councils, the state is equipped to translate national security priorities into achievable regional- and district-level actions while providing feedback that shapes national policy decisions. This two-way information flow improves early warning and evidence-based decision-making and keeps the National Security Strategy abreast of security issues. The WoG approach provides a model through which coordination can be used to enhance policy implementation through collaboration and unity of action. The importance of mandate, accountability and coordination is highlighted through the SSG Theory. This ensures that the implementation of national security policies has clear, successful objectives. Combined with the Human Security Theory, these theories ensure implementation focuses on state and people’s security. [iii] Enhanced Regional and International Cooperation Ghana’s National Security Strategy can be successfully implemented both within and beyond its borders, because contemporary security risks are transnational and, therefore, demand joint action. Based on the creation of an integrated national intelligence structure, the Act enhances Ghana’s ability to cooperate on security issues with bilateral, multilateral and regional security partners. The Act strengthens intelligence cooperation with regional and international partners to facilitate timely exchange of intelligence on terrorism, violent extremism, transnational organised crime, cybercrime, maritime insecurity, trafficking and other cross-border threats. Such institutional coherence improves Ghana’s ability to participate in security and intelligence-sharing arrangements under the ECOWAS, AU and the UN, thereby contributing to collective regional security. The Act also enhances Ghana’s capacity to fulfil its international security commitments. Coordination at the national level equips Ghana to operationalise its counterterrorism measures regionally and internationally, and to support peace and security measures. and assist in joint border management, maritime security and transnational crime prevention. This enhances regional stability while safeguarding Ghana’s national interests in the face of the increasing interconnectivity in the security domain. Realism identifies regional cooperation as an approach through which countries can protect their national interests from common external threats, while SSG emphasises the point that professional and coordinated institutions tend to cooperate internationally. The WoG Approach also emphasises the importance of effective national institutions for effective international cooperation. Professionalism of Intelligence Agencies Regional and international cooperation becomes sustainable when intelligence bodies are professional, competent and credible. In this context, Act 1168 immensely improves Ghana’s security as far as the professionalism of its intelligence agencies is concerned. Professional intelligence agencies play an important role in improving intelligence gathering and analysis, operational effectiveness and creating public trust, which are crucial for national security. One significant implication of Act 1168 is the provision of a well-defined legal and institutional framework on the structure and mandate of intelligence agencies. As Act 1168 outlines the responsibilities of the Internal Intelligence Agency, External Intelligence Agency and Signals Intelligence Agency, established by Act 1040, it helps in minimising ambiguities and specialisation, leading to efficient functioning. Further still, the Act enhances professionalism by enhancing accountability, ethics and compliance with the rule of law. It requires intelligence operatives to conduct themselves in line with legal frameworks that entail effective operations within constitutional principles and democratic accountability. Professionalism, institutional discipline and compliance with human rights values are encouraged through these legal frameworks. These values minimise the chances of political interference and abuse of intelligence powers. SSG is the central theory with which one can understand these reforms, since it emphasises professionalism, accountability, civilian control and effectiveness as key features of democratic security institutions. The WoG theory complements this position because it acknowledges that professional intelligence services are crucial for proper interagency coordination and evidence-based decision-making. The Human Security Theory further emphasises that professional intelligence services enhance the safety of citizens through lawful and preventive measures against threats. Anticipated Challenges Affecting the Effectiveness of the Act. Despite the substantial improvements introduced by Act 1168 to Ghana’s existing national security structure, the success of the Act in achieving its objectives depends on the effective implementation of the Act. This is because enhancing national resilience under the Act is only possible if the above-mentioned reforms are complemented with appropriate resources and effective interagency collaboration. One potential major challenge is coordination. Even though Act 1168 provides clear procedures for coordination through the National Security Council, the National Security Coordinator and the regional and district security councils, rivalries and competition within bureaucracies threaten intelligence sharing and collaboration. Thus, building trust among agencies and developing a good communication system remain crucial. Resource and capacity constraints are also an important risk factor. Good intelligence gathering, cybersecurity, surveillance technologies, data analysis and professional training demand considerable funding and qualified human resources. Insufficient funds, lack of appropriate technology and lack of qualified personnel may jeopardise the operations of intelligence and security agencies. Another challenge is finding a balance between national security and democracy on the one hand and human rights on the other. Intelligence agencies enjoy specialised powers which require constant checks to ensure such powers are not abused, politicised or erode public trust. SSG underlines the point that efficient institutions must be accountable, professional and subject to democratic control, whereas the WoG approach underscores the significance of sustained cooperation among governmental institutions. These perspectives indicate that mere legal reforms do not ensure effective national security results unless accompanied by improved institutional capabilities. Conclusion and Policy Recommendations The Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2026 (Act 1168) is a major milestone in ensuring a robust national security system in Ghana by creating a legal and institutional structure to deal with modern security threats. This has been shown throughout this paper, where it is evident that the Act improves national security by improving strategic coordination, intelligence gathering and analysis, counterterrorism capability, democratic governance, respect for human rights, cybersecurity, protection of critical national infrastructure, crisis management, implementation of the National Security Strategy, regional and international cooperation and professionalism of intelligence agencies. The Act is an intelligent and holistic approach to security issues. Enhancing national security, components such as the Office of the National Security Coordinator and the regional and district security councils result in decision-making, collaboration and decentralised security governance. However, no less significant is the reinforcement of democratic principles, civilian control and constitutionalism because democracy and national security are closely linked. However, the success of Act 1168 depends on how it is implemented. Possible constraints to its full effectiveness include resource challenges, technology constraints, political rivalry, intelligence-sharing obstacles and emerging cyberthreats. To derive maximum advantage from the Act, the government must focus on coordinating the work of agencies by developing effective intelligence and communication systems and standard procedures. Professional development, intelligence technologies, cybersecurity and strategic analysis should be advanced for better operations. Moreover, democratic oversight by the executive, legislature, judiciary and other accountability institutions must also be improved to ensure intelligence operations conform to the Constitution and human rights. Lastly, regional and district security councils must be empowered for early warning and preventative security, and the state must also consistently improve cooperation with ECOWAS, AU and others on intelligence issues.

items.title: Béja | Découvertes archéologiques sur le site de Henchir Matria à Teboursouk
items.description: Dans le cadre d’une convention de coopération internationale avec l’Université de Sassari (Italie), l’Institut national du patrimoine a mené une campagne de fouilles archéologiques sur le site de Henchir Matria, situé au nord de Teboursouk, dans le gouvernorat de Béja, du 6 septembre 2026 au 4 octobre 2026. Des chercheurs et des étudiants de différents niveaux ont pris part aux travaux et ont tous œuvré dans une parfaite harmonie à l’étude et à la mise en valeur de deux secteurs principaux de la ville antique connue sous le nom de Numluli. Le premier secteur comprend le Capitole, construit en 170 apr. J.-C. L’équipe y a mis au jour le dallage de la place publique, une fontaine ainsi que de nombreux éléments architecturaux et décoratifs du temple (chapiteaux, colonnes, décors géométriques variés et fragments de statues, etc.), qui remontent tous à la période romaine. Le second secteur comprend une basilique vandale construite au milieu du Ve siècle apr. J.-C. Elle abrite des sépultures de notables chrétiens, différentes salles, des murs, ainsi que des jarres funéraires et des jarres implantées verticalement destinées au stockage des provisions. Le secteur a également livré des panneaux de mosaïque. INP L’article Béja | Découvertes archéologiques sur le site de Henchir Matria à Teboursouk est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Allemagne – Sénégal: de Senghor à Faye, six décennies d’une relation forte
items.description: Depuis l’établissement de leurs relations diplomatiques en 1960, l’Allemagne et le Sénégal ont construit une coopération qui n’a cessé de se diversifier. Au fil des décennies et des changements de contexte, ce partenariat s’est renouvelé pour investir, aujourd’hui, de nouveaux champs, notamment l’industrie, l’énergie et la formation professionnelle. Une des rues de Fann-Résidence à Dakar, porte le nom de Léo Frobénius. Pourquoi l’avoir baptisée du nom de l’ethnologue allemand ? C’est qu’à côté de ses compagnons dans la négritude, Aimé Césaire et de Léon-Gontran Damas, le Président Senghor tenait à saluer un penseur qui l’a personnellement influencé. En effet, chez le président-poète, l’influence allemande participe à la formation d’une pensée qui cherche à « articuler raison, intuition, culture et connaissance ». Et Léo Frobenius y occupe une place singulière. Senghor lui attribuait une contribution telle qu’il considérait que Frobenius avait contribué à réhabiliter à ses yeux la « raison intuitive », comme l’a souligné le philosophe Souleymane Bachir Diagne dans son ouvrage intitulé « Léopold Sédar Senghor : l’art africain comme philosophie », (Riveneuve, Paris, 2007). Dans un entretien accordé au Soleil en août 2018 à l’occasion de la visite de la Chancelière Angela Merkel au Sénégal, le défunt Pr Maguèye Kassé expliquait que Senghor avait créé le Département de Langues et Civilisations germaniques de l’Université de Dakar en 1973 sous l’inspiration de Léon Frobenius. « Par ses humanités, Senghor était en confrontation avec la culture allemande. Il s’est pris une affection particulière pour l’Allemagne, ses traditions et ses mythes, notamment le culte de la terre, de l’homme et de la nature qui, selon lui, rapprocheraient le Négro-Africain de l’Allemand ». Se dessine ainsi une première histoire, peu connue, des liens entre l’Allemagne et le Sénégal : celle de la rencontre d’idées ayant accompagné celle des États. Il y a des dates qui résument à elles seules la profondeur d’une relation. Le 23 septembre 1960 en est une pour les deux pays. Quelques mois après l’accession du Sénégal à la souveraineté internationale, Dakar et la République fédérale d’Allemagne (RFA) établissent leurs relations diplomatiques. L’Allemagne a été le troisième pays à reconnaître officiellement le Sénégal comme le mentionne la plaque d’immatriculation diplomatique (003). La coopération allemande au développement prend ainsi racine dès les premières années de l’indépendance. Léopold Sédar Senghor devient le premier Président de la République, tandis qu’à Bonn, Konrad Adenauer dirige la RFA depuis 1949. Si une rencontre directe entre Senghor et Adenauer n’est pas établie par les sources disponibles, les deux dirigeants appartiennent à une génération soucieuse de reconstruire, après les traumatismes de la guerre et du totalitarisme, un ordre politique fondé sur l’État de droit, avec les préoccupations et contextes propres à chacun. Sur le terrain institutionnel, la relation se consolide. Un accord de protection des investissements est signé en 1966 et la coopération culturelle se développe. En pleine guerre froide, Dakar franchit une étape supplémentaire en établissant, le 22 août 1973, des relations diplomatiques avec la République démocratique allemande (RDA). Le Sénégal entretient dès lors des relations avec les deux Allemagnes, tout en maintenant un lien privilégié avec Bonn. L’ouverture de son ambassade à Bonn au milieu des années 1970 confirme cette volonté. En 1977, Senghor se rend en RFA et est notamment reçu par le président fédéral Walter Scheel. L’année suivante, Willy Brandt, ancien chancelier devenu président de l’Internationale socialiste, se rend à Dakar. La relation s’étend alors à plusieurs domaines : coopération économique, culture, éducation et dialogue Nord-Sud. L’arrivée d’Abdou Diouf à la présidence, en 1981, ne modifie pas cette trajectoire. En mars 1986, il est reçu en Allemagne par le chancelier Helmut Kohl et rencontre le président fédéral Richard von Weizsäcker. En octobre 1987, le ministre allemand des Affaires étrangères Hans-Dietrich Genscher effectue une visite à Dakar. Paix, droits de l’homme et règlement pacifique des conflits figurent parmi les thèmes du dialogue. Le Sénégal s’affirme alors comme un partenaire politique stable en Afrique de l’Ouest. Puis l’Histoire s’accélère. La chute du mur de Berlin, le 9 novembre 1989, et la réunification de l’Allemagne, le 3 octobre 1990, mettent fin à la coexistence des deux États allemands. Pour Dakar, cette nouvelle donne signifie le retour à un interlocuteur unique : l’Allemagne réunifiée. Cela ne remet pas en cause les acquis de trois décennies de coopération. Sous Abdoulaye Wade, le partenariat prend une coloration plus économique. En septembre 2006, le Président sénégalais rencontre à Berlin le Président Horst Köhler et la chancelière Angela Merkel. Aux questions de développement et d’investissement s’ajoute désormais celle des migrations, avec la recherche de réponses communes aux départs irréguliers vers l’Europe. Avec Macky Sall, le partenariat change encore d’échelle. Reçu par Angela Merkel à Berlin en mars 2014, le Président sénégalais revient quatre ans plus tard sur la relation bilatérale avec la visite officielle de la chancelière allemande à Dakar, le 29 août 2018. Développement, investissements, coopération régionale et création d’emplois sont au cœur des échanges. En janvier 2020, Macky Sall a été de nouveau reçu à Berlin. La visite du Président fédéral Frank-Walter Steinmeier à Dakar, en février 2022, ouvre une autre séquence. Il est présent à l’inauguration du stade Abdoulaye Wade de Diamniadio. Dans un Sahel marqué par les crises sécuritaires, le dialogue porte notamment sur le Mali et la stabilité régionale. L’Allemagne apparaît désormais non seulement comme un partenaire économique, mais aussi comme un acteur engagé sur les questions de sécurité et de stabilité. La visite de Bassirou Diomaye Faye à Berlin, du 21 au 23 juin 2026, prolonge cette longue histoire. Reçu par Frank-Walter Steinmeier et le chancelier Friedrich Merz, le Chef de l’État sénégalais place l’économie, l’industrie, l’énergie et la formation professionnelle au cœur de son agenda. Les deux dirigeants saluent la solidité d’une relation fondée sur « une amitié cordiale et une estime réciproque », comme le souligne Le Soleil. Dakar entend attirer davantage d’entreprises allemandes et inscrire le partenariat dans les priorités de la « Vision Sénégal 2050 ». Berlin, de son côté, souligne le rôle du Sénégal dans la stabilité de la sous-région et la coopération sécuritaire. De Senghor à Faye, la relation germano-sénégalaise a traversé les bouleversements de l’Histoire sans rompre son fil conducteur. De Bonn à Berlin, de la coopération au développement aux enjeux économiques, énergétiques et sécuritaires, le partenariat s’est adapté sans perdre sa substance. En 1968, Senghor voyait dans la présence de Lübke « une amitié entre nos deux peuples ». Près de six décennies plus tard, Faye et Merz en célèbrent encore la solidité. Les époques ont changé. Le lien demeure. Samboudian KAMARA

items.title: NYSC abduction: Mother demands airlift, security escorts for corps members nationwide
items.description: By Adeola Badru The abduction of 20 prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members travelling to their orientation camps has triggered fresh calls for the Federal Government to overhaul the transportation and security arrangements for young graduates deployed across the country for national service. The call came as the 20 prospective corps members, who were abducted in Imo State, returned safely to Ibadan on Thursday after seven days in captivity and were taken to the Department of State Services (DSS) headquarters in the Aleshinloye area of the city for debriefing. The mother of one of the rescued corps members, Faith Felicia Abiala, said the incident had exposed the dangers faced by young graduates travelling long distances by road to fulfil their national service obligations. Abiala, who described her daughter’s safe return as a moment of overwhelming relief, urged the government to provide stronger security arrangements for corps members travelling to their states of deployment or consider transporting them by air. “My advice to the government is that when Corps members are posted to their service states, they should ensure proper security arrangements, or allow them to travel by air to avoid these kinds of dangerous road journeys,” she said. The mother recalled the emotional trauma that followed the abduction of her daughter, saying she was so devastated when she received the news that she could not eat. “I cannot recount all the tears and sorrow, but I give thanks to God that I am seeing her alive today. On the day she was taken, I was so devastated I couldn’t even eat, but today my heart is filled with joy,” Abiala said. She also commended the DSS and the security teams from Oyo and Imo states for their efforts in securing the victims’ return. “I thank God, and I thank the DSS officials—they really tried! The team from Oyo State and the team from Imo State, they really tried and stood by us until our children came out safe and sound,” she said. Another relative of one of the victims, Alhaja Alimot Akande described their release as a major relief after days of uncertainty. “It is good news! Good news! Good news!” she said. She said the confirmation of the victims’ release finally enabled their families to sleep peacefully after days of anguish. “Ah! Immediately I heard they were released yesterday, I slept soundly!” Akande said. The abductors had reportedly demanded N50 million for each of the 20 victims, amounting to N1 billion, before the demand was allegedly reduced to N5 million per victim, bringing the total to N100 million. The parents had earlier visited the private residence of the Olubadan of Ibadanland, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, in Ibadan, seeking his intervention in securing the release of their children. The Oyo State Commissioner of Police, Olugbenga Abimbola, and the Aseyin of Iseyinland, Oba Sefiu Adeyeri, were also involved in efforts to secure the victims’ release. The Olubadan subsequently announced the freedom of the prospective corps members after receiving confirmation from Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodinma. “The kidnapped graduates have been released. The Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodinma, confirmed this in a telephone conversation at about 5.00pm,” Ladoja stated in a statement issued by his media aide, Adeola Oloko. The 20 victims were among 30 prospective corps members travelling in two buses from Oyo State towards orientation camps in Abia State when gunmen attacked them along the Owerri-Onitsha Road in Umunoha, Mbaitoli Local Government Area of Imo State. Ten of the prospective corps members escaped into the bush during the attack and subsequently made their way to safety, while the remaining 20 were abducted. The victims spent seven days in captivity before regaining their freedom and being brought back to Ibadan, where they were received at the DSS facility. The incident had generated widespread anxiety among their parents and relatives, with the families seeking intervention from government officials, security agencies and traditional rulers. items.title: Le Parlement européen appelle à examiner l’inscription des Frères musulmans sur la liste terroriste
items.description: Le Parlement européen a adopté, à une large majorité, une résolution invitant l’Union européenne à étudier l’inscription officielle des Frères musulmans sur la liste des organisations terroristes et à engager des actions contre les réseaux, les financements et les structures qui leur sont associés, dans la perspective d’une réponse coordonnée à l’échelle européenne. Le texte a été approuvé par 381 voix, contre 167, tandis que 15 députés se sont abstenus. Il préconise aussi l'exclusion définitive au sein des institutions européennes de Femyso (Forum des organisations européennes musulmanes de jeunes et d'étudiants), association considérée comme proche des Frères musulmans. Ce vote ne constitue toutefois pas, à ce stade, une décision définitive et contraignante en faveur de l’inscription de l’organisation sur la liste européenne des entités terroristes. Il traduit plutôt la volonté du Parlement européen de promouvoir une stratégie commune au sein de l’Union, en lieu et place d’approches nationales menées séparément par les États membres. Sur le plan institutionnel, le Parlement européen dispose d’un pouvoir d’influence politique, mais ne peut, à lui seul, prononcer une telle inscription. Si des fondements juridiques établissant une implication de l’organisation dans des activités terroristes venaient à être réunis, le dossier serait alors transmis au Conseil de l’Union européenne, compétent pour adopter une décision contraignante. Selon le texte, la France est à l’avant-garde des efforts européens dans ce dossier. Paris plaide notamment pour l’établissement d’une cartographie des réseaux des Frères musulmans en Europe, l’identification de leurs sources de financement, une meilleure connaissance de leur réseau politique ainsi qu’un renforcement du contrôle des fonds européens accordés à des associations susceptibles d’agir comme des structures de façade. D'ailleurs, un rapport publié en mai 2025 sur l'islamisme politique avait mis en garde contre un entrisme « par le bas », au niveau local et associatif, mené par les Frères musulmans. Ce sujet est déjà porté par une partie de la droite et de l'extrême droite dans le cadre de la campagne pour l'élection présidentielle de 2027. The post Le Parlement européen appelle à examiner l’inscription des Frères musulmans sur la liste terroriste appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Campus France en Guinée : refus de visa, absence de motifs détaillés… l’ambassadeur français s’explique
items.description: Pourquoi certaines demandes de visa étudiant sont-elles refusées après une procédure Campus France ? Et pourquoi les candidats ne reçoivent-ils pas toujours une explication détaillée des motifs de ces refus ? La question a été posée à Luc Briard, ambassadeur de France en Guinée et en Sierra Leone, lors de la conférence de presse qui a suivi, ce jeudi 8 octobre 2026 à Conakry, le lancement de la campagne « Études en France » 2026-2027. En réponse, le diplomate a d’abord rappelé que l’accompagnement par Campus France ou l’admission dans un établissement français ne garantit pas automatiquement l’obtention d’un visa. « Simplement, il n’y a pas un droit au visa. Voilà », a-t-il déclaré. Concernant l’absence de communication de motifs détaillés aux demandeurs, Luc Briard a expliqué que les informations actuellement disponibles sur les refus de visa restent générales et ne permettent pas une communication individualisée au cas par cas. « Il est vrai que nous avons des mesures d’information sur les refus de visa qui sont génériques, qui ne peuvent pas être individuelles », a-t-il précisé. L’ambassadeur a toutefois annoncé une possible évolution dans la communication autour de ces refus. Les services français travaillent notamment sur une restitution globale des principales catégories de motifs ayant conduit à des refus, afin de permettre aux candidats de mieux comprendre les difficultés rencontrées dans leurs démarches. « En revanche, nous pourrons faire, et ça on va y travailler, nous pouvons faire une restitution globale sur les grandes typologies de refus », a-t-il annoncé. Pour Luc Briard, cette démarche répond à un souci de transparence et pourrait contribuer à renforcer la confiance des étudiants et de leurs familles dans la procédure. « C’est un exercice de transparence auquel on peut tout à fait se prêter parce qu’il est utile pour améliorer la confiance dans le système », a-t-il conclu. Cette clarification intervient au lendemain du lancement en Guinée de la campagne « Études en France » 2026-2027. À cette occasion, les responsables de Campus France ont appelé les candidats à mieux préparer leurs dossiers, à veiller à la cohérence de leurs projets d’études et à rester vigilants face aux pratiques frauduleuses. Mayi Cissé L’article Campus France en Guinée : refus de visa, absence de motifs détaillés… l’ambassadeur français s’explique est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Transparence extractive : Le Sénégal sacré à Bruxelles par le EITI Chair’s Award 2026
items.description: Ce jeudi 8 octobre 2026, à l’occasion de la Conférence mondiale de l’Initiative pour la Transparence dans les Industries Extractives (ITIE) organisée à Bruxelles, le pays s’est vu décerner le prestigieux EITI Chair’s Award 2026. Cette distinction internationale vient consacrer un engagement constant et des progrès remarquables en matière de transparence, de redevabilité et de gestion responsable des secteurs minier, pétrolier et gazier.Le ministre de l’Énergie et du Pétrole, El Hadji Abdourahmane Diouf, a reçu ce prix d’excellence au nom de l’État du Sénégal lors d’une cérémonie solennelle devant le cénacle des décideurs mondiaux du secteur extractif. Thialy Faye, président du CN-ITIE, a souligné que «cette appréciation internationale illustre la synergie parfaite entre les autorités, le secteur privé et la société civile pour faire de la transparence un levier concret de développement».En réaffirmant sa volonté de poursuivre cette gouvernance inclusive et durable, le Sénégal transforme la gestion de son sous-sol en modèle d’intégration démocratique. Conçus pour mettre à l’honneur les nations et les acteurs ayant fait preuve d’un leadership politique audacieux et soutenu, les EITI Chair’s Awards traduisent une reconnaissance explicite des réformes courageuses menées par Dakar pour conformer son cadre juridique et opérationnel aux exigences internationales les plus rigoureuses. Fatou NGOM (Stagiaire)

items.title: Un député : « le renouvellement de l’accord de pêche avec l’UE nécessite la protection des intérêts de la Mauritanie »
items.description: Le député Mohamed Bouya Cheikh Mohamed Fadel a déclaré que le renouvellement de l'accord de pêche entre la Mauritanie et l'Union européenne nécessitait de définir les intérêts mauritaniens et de fournir aux négociateurs des expertises techniques précises sur ce que souhaite la Mauritanie et ce qui peut être accepté dans l'accord. Le député a ajouté, sur sa page Facebook, que la révision de l’accord devrait porter sur la durée de celui-ci, les quantités et les espèces de poissons, la contrepartie financière, les conditions de travail et les droits des pêcheurs mauritaniens, ainsi que l’amélioration des conditions d’immigration légale. Le député a appelé à étudier la possibilité de lier l’accord à l’exportation des produits nationaux vers les marchés européens, au financement des infrastructures maritimes, au déchargement dans les ports nationaux, ainsi qu’à la formation continue dans le domaine de la pêche et des activités maritimes. Il a déclaré que l’accord nécessitait l’intervention d’experts techniques et des études approfondies sur son contenu avant d’être signé ou soumis à l’Assemblée nationale pour ratification, appelant à la sélection d’une délégation de négociation et à sa mise en possession des informations nécessaires. La Mauritanie possède un littoral atlantique s’étendant sur plus de 700 kilomètres et compte parmi les zones les plus poissonneuses du monde, tandis que des flottes de pêche européennes, chinoises, turques et japonaises se disputent ses ressources, dans un contexte de craintes quant à l’épuisement des stocks halieutiques. La Mauritanie est liée depuis des décennies à un accord de pêche avec l’Union européenne, renouvelé périodiquement, qui prévoit le versement par l’Union d’environ 57,5 millions d’euros par an en échange des droits d’accès aux eaux mauritaniennes pour la pêche, ainsi que 3,3 millions d’euros par an pour soutenir les communautés locales, la recherche et les infrastructures dans le secteur de la pêche.

items.title: La Fiscalía pide 12 años de cárcel para el médico que atendió antes de su muerte a Maradona
items.description: La Fiscalía argentina sostiene que Diego Armando Maradona murió el 25 de noviembre de 2020 por la negligencia del equipo médico que lo cuidó en sus últimos días. Según la acusación, el principal responsable de la muerte del astro del fútbol argentino fue su médico personal, el neurocirujano Leopoldo Duque . Hizo “todo lo posible para que todo saliera mal”, aseguró este jueves el fiscal Patricio Ferrari en el alegato final del juicio por la muerte de Maradona. Pidió al tribunal que lo condene a 12 años de prisión por homicidio simple con dolo eventual. La acusación sostiene que Luque sabía el riesgo que corría la salud de Maradona, pudo haber intervenido para evitarlo y, sin embargo, no lo hizo. La acusación pública -integrada también por el fiscal Cosme Iribarre- solicitó además 10 años de cárcel para la coordinadora de la aseguradora privada de salud Swiss Medical, Nancy Forlini, y ocho para la psiquiatra Agustina Cosachov. items.description: Muchos dicen que llevan todo el día viendo en bucle imágenes de ella. Otros la han pensado de camino al trabajo. O a la vuelta. Hay quienes ayer sintieron la necesidad de escribirle algo, pero no salían las palabras. Un “muchas gracias” es lo que les pedía el corazón. La rabia les hizo añadir los “lucharemos nosotros por ti” o “un piso, un techo, una cama, agua”. Y algunos más duros, hartos: “A Maricarmen la mataron”. Negro sobre pedazos de cartón, en hojas sueltas, con spray sobre una lona. Los colocaron sobre sus tiendas y los han llevado a la marcha que este jueves ha reunido a unas 20.000 personas en el centro de Madrid, según la Delegación del Gobierno, para honrar a Maricarmen Abascal, la mujer que les impulsó a tomar la calle , a plantar la primera tienda y 1.000 más. Seguir leyendo
